meta.title: The One Spot Where Four Countries Almost Meet
meta._convention: Duration omitted per beat -- filled from measured narration length. Verified via WebSearch before scripting: Kazungula quadripoint ~17.793S,25.260E, where the Zambezi and Chobe rivers meet, ~70km west of Livingstone, Zambia; Botswana/Zambia/Zimbabwe/Namibia all converge within meters of each other here (survey consensus is actually two adjacent tripoints, not one true quadripoint -- the beat 5 twist). All four country codes (BW=72, ZM=894, ZW=716, NA=516) confirmed present both in country-codes.json and in the world-atlas 110m dataset by direct node lookup, so highlight is used (unlike the other non-country Day 23-29 topics).

beats.voText: Four countries almost touch at this single spot on the Zambezi River, the closest thing on Earth to a true four-country meeting point.
Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Namibia all converge here, at Kazungula, where the Zambezi and Chobe rivers meet in southern Africa.
International law technically doesn't recognize true quadripoints, so surveyors have argued for decades over exactly which two countries touch in the middle.
For decades, a car ferry was the only way to cross between them, travelers could hop borders in minutes, where four nations nearly meet.
In 2021, a new bridge finally replaced the ferry, but the old survey dispute never got resolved, it's really two tripoints, not one true quadripoint.
Four countries, one river, and a border puzzle surveyors still can't fully agree on. Follow for more places on Earth that shouldn't exist, but do.
